column4: The lexicon's water-side example is people returning in separate groups; here يَصْدُرُ النَّاسُ أَشْتَاتًا stages that dispersal on the Day and says they are shown their deeds.
The section treats سَعْي as every good or evil effort; this verse makes a person's share depend on مَا سَعَىٰ.
The next verse says سَعْيَهُ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ; it directly joins the section's effort to its image of deeds becoming visible.
The linked verse gives the full recompense after the striving is seen, completing the effort-to-outcome sequence behind the two paths.
This verse names the one who desires the Hereafter and سَعَىٰ لَهَا سَعْيَهَا, then says that effort is appreciated; 17:18 supplies the contrasting worldly aim.
The section's opening سَعْي is recalled when the great calamity makes a person remember مَا سَعَىٰ.
The فَأَمَّا opening introduces a transgressing type, as the section's paired فَأَمَّا/وَأَمَّا clauses sort divergent efforts; the next verses identify this type's preference and end.
Choosing الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا is the opposite orientation to the giver whose course is toward God's pleasure and the Hereafter; 79:39 names its end.
The linked side of the two-way account ends at الْجَحِيمَ, supplying the destination for the person who preferred worldly life.
The second وَأَمَّا type fears his Lord's standing and restrains desire, a concrete reversal of the transgressor's preference in 79:37–38 and a close parallel to the God-fearing path.
For the God-fearing side, this verse names Paradise as its resting place, completing the paired destinations.
النَّجْدَيْنِ gives the section's two ways a concrete counterpart: a human being is shown two elevated routes.
The verse says God guided the human to السَّبِيلَ, then divides the response into grateful and ungrateful, making the section's two directed courses explicit.
قَصْدُ السَّبِيلِ is set against a deviating way, while guidance is attributed to God; this states the straight-versus-crooked boundary in the section.
This verse says communities have distinct law and way, commands فَاسْتَبِقُوا الْخَيْرَاتِ, and says all return to God; it brings divergence, directed striving, and its end together.
وجهة, turning toward it, and فَاسْتَبِقُوا الْخَيْرَاتِ occur together here, matching the section's meeting of direction and race.
The command to follow صِرَاطِي مُسْتَقِيمًا and not follow other paths makes the section's straight course and divergent alternatives a direct choice.
The prayer اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ directly voices the need for guidance onto a way.
The next verse defines the requested way through those favored and contrasts them with the angered and astray, giving moral content to the route in 1:6.
قَد تَّبَيَّنَ الرُّشْدُ مِنَ الْغَيِّ marks a boundary between right direction and error, illuminating the section's two distinct courses.
Those who strive for God are promised guidance to سُبُلَنَا; the verse joins exertion to God's direction through multiple ways.
The speakers say God has guided them سُبُلَنَا, then resolve to endure and trust Him; this links the section's plural paths with guidance and the response of trust.
The person who desires the fleeting life is given a limited portion and then faces Hell; 17:19 contrasts the afterlife-directed striving, paralleling the section's two aims and outcomes.
The verse says each acts according to his own شَاكِلَتِهِ and God knows best who is better guided; this gives individual conduct a distinct direction, as in the section's divergent efforts.
The command to follow the clear شَرِيعَة and not people's desires presents a prepared way and a choice about which course to follow.
The contrast between one walking face-down and one walking upright on a straight path makes moral direction visible as bodily movement.
وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ is the same promise of facilitation as the section's path-making verb, addressed to the Prophet.
For one who believes and acts well, this verse promises the best reward and يسرًا; it links a good course to ease, unlike the section's difficult course.
كادحٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ ... فَمُلَاقِيهِ depicts a person striving toward the Lord and meeting Him, a direct image of effort with an endpoint.
The command سَابِقُوا إِلَىٰ مَغْفِرَةٍ and a Garden makes racing toward a final reward explicit.
سَارِعُوا إِلَىٰ مَغْفِرَةٍ and a Garden gives the section's running a specific righteous destination.
The command فَلْيَتَنَافَسِ الْمُتَنَافِسُونَ makes the section's secondary sense of striving as a contest explicit; its context is the reward of the righteous.
وَالسَّابِقُونَ السَّابِقُونَ names the foremost as racers, matching the section's competitive sense of sa'y.
The next verse identifies those forerunners as the brought-near, supplying what being first in 56:10 leads to.
لِسَعْيِهَا رَاضِيَةٌ joins the section's first action-word سَعْي to its final satisfaction, in one description of the rewarded faces.
These people يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ and are foremost in them, a specific image of directed eagerness toward good.
They يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ while calling in hope and fear, joining swift effort with the section's God-fearing orientation.
قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّىٰ directly connects success with purification, matching the giver who gives wealth to purify himself.
The next verse pairs remembrance of the Lord with prayer, specifying the practice that follows purification in 87:14.
The following contrast names preferring worldly life, the alternative to the purified course.
This verse says the Hereafter is better and more enduring, completing the contrast with worldly preference in 87:16 and the section's first/last horizon.
The one who زَكَّاهَا succeeds; this directly echoes the section's purification through giving.
The next verse says the one who دسَّاهَا fails, setting corruption against the successful self-purification of 91:9.
They fulfill vows and fear a day's evil, matching the section's God-fearing course; 76:8–10 show the giving and motive that follow.
They give food to needy people, orphans, and captives; this gives a concrete form to the section's act of giving wealth.
إِنَّمَا نُطْعِمُكُمْ لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ and rejecting reward or thanks directly match giving for God's face without a favor to repay.
The next verse restates their fear of the difficult Day, completing the motive behind the giving in 76:8–9.
Spending is for one's own good and is done ابتغاء وجه الله; the verse directly connects giving with seeking God's face, as in the section.
One does not attain righteousness until spending what one loves; this specifies the cost of the section's giving.
The command to take charity from people's wealth, تَطْهِيرًا وَتُزَكِّيهِم, directly joins wealth-giving to purification.
The verse calls people to spend and names the one who is stingy; it says withholding harms only the self, exposing the false self-sufficiency paired with miserliness in the section.
What God has given is to be used to seek the Hereafter while doing good; this makes wealth a means of choosing a lasting destination.
Wealth and children are the adornment of worldly life, while enduring good deeds are better in reward and hope; this sharpens the section's contrast between wealth and the course that lasts.
The next account says the record leaves nothing small or great uncounted and that people find their deeds present, making visible the efforts for which they are repaid.
Good is for oneself and evil against oneself, followed by return to the Lord; this states the consequence of the section's divergent good and bad striving.
This person gives up himself seeking God's approval, a close parallel in aim to the section's giver who spends only seeking the Lord's face.
The Messenger says he asks no recompense and points to whoever takes a way to the Lord; this links the section's unrepaid giving with a directed path.
The final reward includes رَّضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ, closely echoing the section's closing promise that the giver will be satisfied.
رَاضِيَةً مَّرْضِيَّةً describes a soul returning to its Lord pleased and pleasing, paralleling the section's final satisfaction.
The next verse says to enter among God's servants, continuing the return of the satisfied soul in 89:28.
The sequence ends with entry into God's Garden, supplying the endpoint after the pleased return in 89:28–29.
لِلَّهِ الْآخِرَةُ وَالْأُولَىٰ gives God both terms the section reads as the two ends of a course and as the life here and hereafter.
The verse calls God الْأَوَّلُ وَالْآخِرُ; this uses the same first/last pair as divine attributes, distinct from the section's temporal or race-end sense.
The verse calls worldly life play and adornment and contrasts it with the lasting Hereafter, giving the section's first/last division a concrete value.
On the Day of Resurrection people يَتَفَرَّقُونَ, a direct parallel to the section's dispersed people and divided directions.
The next verse puts the believers in a garden rejoicing, completing one side of the split in 30:14.
The paired next verse assigns the rejecters to punishment, completing the other side of 30:14.
The command to face the upright religion is followed by the day when people will be separated; it joins orientation to the section's division into courses.
شَتَّىٰ describes hearts that are divided despite appearing united; this transfers the section's dispersal from people on a road to inward separation.
The early forerunners are followed by people who follow them well, and God is pleased with them; this joins the section's racing image to the satisfaction of its ending.
تَوَلَّىٰ عَن ذِكْرِنَا names turning away from God's reminder together with wanting worldly life alone, closely matching the section's denier who turns away.
The next verse speaks of straying from God's way and being guided, completing the directional contrast behind the turn in 53:29.
The person reminded of God's signs فَأَعْرَضَ عَنْهَا turns away and forgets what his hands sent ahead, joining the section's turning away to neglected deeds.
This calls the coming Day يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ, a difficult-day counterpart to the section's hard course; 74:10 specifies for whom it is not easy.
غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ makes the difficulty explicit for disbelievers, setting a hard outcome against the section's easy course.
This condemns spending followed by reminders and injury, or for show; it reverses the section's gift made solely for purification and God's face.
Spending to be seen by people is named here, a specific opposite to the section's giver who seeks only God's face.
This condemns those who split their religion into sects; its schismatic division is a contrasting sense of separation beside the section's varied courses.
The command not to turn one's back in battle uses the turn-away family in a physical retreat sense, contrasting with the section's denier who turns away from guidance.
The next verse gives punishment for turning one's back except for a tactical maneuver, making the physical retreat and its consequence explicit.
فَلَا اقْتَحَمَ الْعَقَبَةَ names the steep pass not taken; 90:10 supplies the two elevations, and this verse makes one morally difficult course concrete.
The next verse asks what the steep pass is, introducing the deeds that define the difficult way after the two heights in 90:10.
Freedom of a slave is the first deed in the steep pass described after 90:12, giving the difficult route a concrete act of care.
Feeding during famine continues the steep-pass deeds and recalls the section's emphasis on giving rather than withholding.
The steep-pass description specifies care for an orphan who is related, continuing the route's acts after 90:14.
It next names a needy person in hardship, extending the concrete acts along the steep route.
Faith and mutual counsel to patience and compassion complete the steep-pass deeds, giving the route a moral and relational character.
Those are called أصحاب الميمنة, the right-hand company; after the path's deeds, the verse names one side of the division.
The next verse names the rejecters as أصحاب المشأمة, the opposite company, completing the split after the steep-pass route.
The following verse gives that opposite side an enclosed fire as destination, completing the two outcomes opened by the routes.
Moses asks وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي, using facilitation for a task rather than a road; it clarifies the section's prepared/eased sense.
Allah's stated wish for ease rather than hardship in fasting uses the same ease/difficulty contrast, though there it concerns a legal burden, not two moral paths.
With hardship comes ease, a specific pairing that complicates the section's image of two divergent courses; here relief accompanies hardship.
The repeated assurance again places ease with hardship, reinforcing that distinct relation rather than the section's forked-road outcome.
Among those inheriting the Book are a wrongdoer, a moderate one, and a foremost one in good deeds; this gives a specific threefold spread of human efforts.
The phrase لَتُرْدِينِ uses the ر د ي family for ruining someone; this is a different, destructive sense beside the section's dictionary image of a horse speeding.
The verse says their assumption فَأَرْدَاكُمْ ruined them; this makes the destructive sense of the section's horse-speed root consequential rather than forward motion.
The promise is described as مَأْتِيًّا, something arriving; this recalls the section's dictionary sense of a finish or endpoint in the ء ت ي family, though the verse speaks of a promised Garden.
The next verse identifies the promised inheritance as the Garden for God's servants who fear Him, supplying the destination after 19:61.
Then he turned back and became arrogant, directly recalling the section's وَتَوَلَّىٰ; the nearby speech gives a concrete rejection.
The following verse records his dismissing the warning as transmitted magic, specifying the denial linked to his turn in 74:23.
The next claim calls it human speech, further stating how this speaker denies the message after turning away.
السَّابِقَاتِ سَبْقًا depicts racers or forerunners; who the agents are is uncertain, but their motion directly recalls the section's competitive running sense.
The verse stages people watering flocks at a well and two women held apart from the crowd, recalling the section's shared watering place; it does not show the later dispersal.
Moses waters the women's flock at that same well, completing the watering scene linked to 28:23 without depicting people leaving in separate bands.
The oath by galloping, panting steeds recalls the section's horse-speed image, though these horses charge rather than race morally or competitively.
The steeds reach the midst of a gathered company, giving the charge in 100:1 a point of arrival; the relation to a race finish remains only an analogy.
فَاسْعَوْا commands people to hasten toward Friday remembrance and leave trade; the same sa'y word now gathers them toward one shared direction.
After prayer, people are told to disperse through the land and seek God's bounty; this reverses the gathering of 62:9 and closely recalls people leaving one watering place for separate aims.

Righteousness is not merely turning faces east or west; the verse defines it through belief, giving wealth, keeping promises, and patience. It links the section's qibla/direction gloss to its moral course of giving.
The question about the changed qibla and the statement that God guides whom He wills to a straight way connect physical orientation with the section's hidaya-as-direction gloss.
The verse says the former qibla was a test of who follows the Messenger; it makes turning toward a direction a choice that reveals one's course.
The command to face the Sacred Mosque wherever one is supplies the physical qibla orientation named alongside direction in the section's hidaya dictionary note.
The choice “whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve” is followed by the fire prepared for wrongdoers, explicitly dividing human courses and outcomes.
The Hour is coming so that every soul may be repaid for what it strives for; this directly joins the section's striving to its final reckoning.
The question introduces the greatest losers in deeds; 18:104 identifies their lost effort and mistaken confidence.
سَعْيُهُمْ فِي الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا names efforts lost in worldly life even while their agents think they act well, a direct contrary path to the section's fruitful striving.
The next verse says those losers denied their Lord's signs and meeting Him, explaining the wasted deeds announced in 18:104.
God begins creation and repeats it, with all returning to Him; this gives a creation-to-return arc beside the section's first and last and its race endpoint.
The verse tells the Messenger that he cannot guide whom he loves, while God guides whom He wills; it specifies divine responsibility in the guidance claim.
Believers are told to fear God, seek a means to Him, and strive in His way; the verse brings taqwa, directed effort, and a path into one command.
Satan says he will sit on God's straight path to obstruct it, making opposition to the guided course explicit.
Satan's approach from before, behind, right, and left recalls the section's dictionary list of direction, front, and back; it shows temptation coming from every side of the path.
God opens one person's chest to Islam but makes another's constricted as though climbing heaven; this gives an inward experience of ease and difficulty alongside the section's route metaphor.
The verse says disbelievers' wealth and children will not avail them against God and names the Fire; this directly echoes the section's question about wealth when a person falls.
The same wealth-and-children formula is applied to disbelievers and followed by the Fire, restating the section's limit on wealth at the end of a course.
Wealth and children will not avail people against God, and they are assigned to the Fire; this is another direct formulation of the failure of wealth in the section's reckoning.
Those who hoard gold and silver without spending in God's way are warned of painful punishment, a direct opposite to the section's giver and a concrete form of miserliness.
The next verse says the hoarded metal will be heated and used to brand its owners, then calls it what they hoarded; it makes the miser's wealth itself part of the outcome.
After receiving God's bounty, these people became miserly and turned away; it joins the section's bukhul and tawalla in one account.
The verse condemns those who withhold God's bounty and calls their assumed good evil; it directly develops the miser's path and its reversal.
It names the stingy, those who urge others to stinginess, and those who conceal God's bounty; this adds concealment and social influence to the section's miserly course.
This verse describes the stingy and those who urge stinginess, then says God is self-sufficient; it exposes the false human self-sufficiency paired with withholding in the section.
Spend from what God provided and whoever is protected from the greed of his own soul succeeds; this directly reverses the section's miserly path.
The verse says people would still withhold even if they owned the treasuries of their Lord's mercy; it gives a concrete form to the section's self-sufficient miser.
The warning not to let wealth and children distract from God's remembrance fits the section's self-sufficient person whose wealth cannot save him.
People are urged to spend from what God provided before death comes, a precise link to the section's giver and its warning about the moment a person falls.
The next verse says no soul's appointed time is delayed and God knows what people do, completing the urgency of spending before death in 63:10.
Those who spend and do not follow the gift with reminders or injury receive reward from their Lord; this directly explains the section's giver who has no favor to be repaid.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, specifying the contrast between sincere giving and a gift used to claim a favor.
Those who spend seeking God's approval and to strengthen themselves are compared to a garden on high ground; the motive directly parallels the section's gift for the Lord's face.
Men and women who give charity are promised multiplied reward, a direct giving-to-recompense parallel to the section's course.
Neither wealth nor children bring people near to God; belief and righteous action do, with multiplied reward. This directly distinguishes the section's wealth from the effort that reaches its end.
Those who spend in ease and hardship are described as God-fearing, joining the section's generosity with its two conditions and its taqwa.
The God-fearing are said to reserve a right in their wealth for the asker and deprived, specifying the generosity of the pious course.
